Gunmen kill at least seven at a church funeral in Jordan in a rare terror attack
items.summary:
At least seven people were killed and about 40 were injured on Friday when gunmen opened fire on mourners at a funeral in the town of Hmoud, in Jordan's southern Karak province. Jordan's public security agency called it a terrorist attack on Christians gathered at St. George's Greek Orthodox Church, and said the attackers had not been captured by Friday afternoon.

Witnesses described more than 150 people inside and around the church when the shooting began in the courtyard and continued for several minutes. Security footage circulating online showed three gunmen, and survivors told reporters they hid behind the altar to escape. King Abdullah visited wounded victims at a hospital, promised a harsh response, and the prime minister declared three days of national mourning with flags at half-staff.

Attacks like this are almost unheard of in Jordan, where Christians make up only about 2 percent of the population and sectarian violence is rare. Officials blamed an extremist ideology that brands other faiths as infidels, and leaders across the region, along with the U.S. embassy, condemned the killings and offered condolences.

A manhunt was still under way Friday evening and no group had claimed responsibility. Watch for arrests, for whether the death toll rises among the seriously wounded, and for how Jordan tightens security around churches and other gathering places in the days ahead.

items.title: Israel seals off Hebron and starts demolitions after two soldiers are killed, four days before its election
items.summary:
Israeli forces began demolishing buildings and ordering residents out of a Hebron neighborhood on Friday, hours after two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a military checkpoint in the West Bank city. Three other soldiers were lightly wounded, and both gunmen were shot and killed at the scene.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu first ordered a full closure of the West Bank, then scaled that back hours later to a possible cordon around Hebron and the nearby city of Halhul. He said the army would evacuate the area around the attack, search house to house, and reshape it completely, using the same approach applied in several West Bank refugee camps in early 2025 that displaced thousands of people. In the Farsh al-Hawa area, demolitions were already under way by Friday afternoon, with one filmed soldier giving a housing complex five minutes to evacuate.

The timing makes the response especially charged. Israel votes on Tuesday in its first election since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack, and Netanyahu has campaigned as a security hardliner. Hamas praised Friday's attack without claiming it, Israeli commanders said a vehicle used by the gunmen held a large amount of ammunition, and the Israeli human rights group B'Tselem condemned the planned evacuations as forced displacement.

Watch how far the Hebron operation expands over the weekend, whether a wider West Bank closure follows, and how the violence lands with voters in the final days before Tuesday's election.

items.title: UN warns 800,000 people in Yemen's Taiz are cut off from aid after 20 days under siege
items.summary:
Aid agencies warned on Friday that Taiz City in Yemen is sliding into a fast-moving humanitarian emergency after being encircled for 20 days by Houthi forces fighting government troops. Roads into the city are cut, very little fuel or food is getting in, and people inside cannot safely get out, the UN aid coordination office said.

The World Food Programme put the number cut off from assistance at more than 800,000, including 600,000 people who depend on humanitarian aid and 200,000 women and children. Because most water in Taiz arrives by truck, closed roads and scarce diesel have cut water production roughly in half and roughly tripled the price of trucked water. UNICEF said it has screened more than 168,000 children in Taiz this year and found more than 52,000 acutely malnourished.

The current escalation began in early September and ended the relative calm that followed a 2022 truce. UN migration figures show about 258,679 people displaced between June and mid-October, most of them in Taiz and Lahj, with many families moving repeatedly into already crowded sites.

The stakes are time-sensitive: therapeutic food stocks can cover roughly three months, but only if supplies can actually reach clinics and families can reach treatment. Watch for any negotiated opening of the roads into Taiz, and for signs the fighting is moving closer to the city's densest neighborhoods.

items.title: Russia's central bank holds rates at 14% and warns inflation will run hotter than expected
items.summary:
Russia's central bank kept its main interest rate at 14 percent on Friday, holding steady for the second time in under two months, and raised its inflation forecast for 2026 to between 7.1 and 7.6 percent, up from 6 to 7 percent. The bank still says it expects inflation to reach its 4 percent target in 2027, but signaled borrowing costs will stay near current levels for some time.

The bank pointed to a mix of pressures keeping prices high: heavy government spending, higher utility fees, and Ukrainian drone attacks that have knocked refineries out of action. Petrol prices are up 21 percent since the start of the year and diesel 13.4 percent, with queues reported at fuel stations, and consumer prices overall are up 6.2 percent so far in 2026 compared with 4.8 percent in the same period last year.

Markets took the tougher outlook poorly. Moscow's main stock index fell about 1.3 percent after the decision, bond prices also slipped, and analysts described the revised forecast as a harsh downgrade of what lies ahead, even though the rouble itself strengthened against the dollar.

For ordinary Russians, the message is that expensive credit and rising fuel costs are not ending soon. Watch whether refinery repairs ease the fuel crunch, or whether another rate decision has to reckon with inflation expectations that the bank itself says remain stubbornly high.

items.title: Economists now expect Canada's central bank to raise rates next week, reversing months of forecasts
items.summary:
A majority of economists polled by Reuters now expect the Bank of Canada to raise its overnight rate by a quarter point to 2.50 percent on October 28, and to raise it once more by the end of March. Nineteen of 34 economists surveyed between October 21 and 23 took that view — a sharp turn from the previous poll, in which about 80 percent expected the bank to hold at 2.25 percent through the end of 2026.

The shift followed public remarks last weekend by Governor Tiff Macklem that markets read as a hint a hike was coming, and a new business outlook survey showing inflation expectations rising sharply. Canadian inflation came in at 3.1 percent in September, just above the central bank's 1 to 3 percent target range, and interest-rate futures moved from pricing about a 30 percent chance of an October hike to roughly three-in-four.

Analysts say the survey evidence appears to have changed the governor's tone and theirs at the same time: businesses and consumers expecting higher prices can help make those prices real, which is exactly what a pre-emptive hike is meant to head off. The bank will also publish updated quarterly inflation forecasts alongside next week's decision.

If the bank does move, it would be its first rate change in a year, and it would land while trade talks with the United States — Canada's main export market — remain unsettled. Watch the October 28 statement for how explicitly the bank commits to a second increase.

items.title: India's business growth hits a four-month high in October, but hiring stalls
items.summary:
Business activity in India expanded at its fastest pace in four months in October, according to a preliminary purchasing managers' survey released Friday. The composite index rose to 56.7 from 55.9 in September, comfortably above the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction and ahead of the 56.1 forecast in a Reuters poll.

Services drove the improvement, with that index climbing to 56.2 from 55.2 on stronger demand. Manufacturing output also grew, though its headline reading eased slightly to 54.9 from 55.1. Export orders expanded at the fastest pace in six months, led by goods producers, while foreign demand for services softened.

The soft spot was jobs. Employment was unchanged in October, ending a nine-month run of hiring, as companies said current staffing could handle the extra work — and backlogs fell at one of the fastest rates in more than six years. Price pressures also cooled, with input-cost inflation at its lowest in almost a year and selling-price increases the weakest since March of last year.

Growth without hiring is the tension to watch in the world's most populous economy. If orders keep rising while payrolls stay flat, pressure will build either to hire in coming months or to accept longer hours and thinner service — and the next few surveys will show which way firms choose.

items.title: Trump promises a $5,000 'Trump dividend' to every adult citizen if Republicans win Congress
items.summary:
President Donald Trump used his Friday afternoon rally in Fort Myers to float a new closing pitch for the midterms: a $5,000 payment to every adult U.S. citizen, which he called the Trump dividend, if Republicans keep the House and win the Senate on November 3. He spoke for about 90 minutes to a packed Alico Arena at Florida Gulf Coast University before departing for Mar-a-Lago.

Trump said tariff revenue and economic growth would pay for the plan, with one condition — the money would have to be spent inside the United States. He compared the idea to a $1,776 payment his administration previously directed to military personnel. The rest of the speech stumped for Florida Republicans, especially gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds and Senate candidate Ashley Moody, attacked Democrat David Jolly on guns, and hinted at another possible round of strikes on Iran.

No bill text, cost estimate, or administration detail accompanied the promise, and a payout of that size to every adult citizen would require congressional approval and run into the trillions of dollars. That gap between a rally pledge and an actual program is why the reaction in the final 11 days matters more than the number itself.

Watch for whether Republican candidates adopt the pledge, whether the White House puts any structure behind it, and how Democrats price it out in response. Trump continues the barnstorm in Georgia on Saturday and Michigan on Sunday.

items.title: Attorney General won't rule out Justice Department blocking a state from certifying election results
items.summary:
Attorney General Todd Blanche declined on Thursday to rule out the Justice Department trying to block a state from certifying its midterm election results. Asked directly, he said there are hypothetical scenarios — he offered a doomsday scenario as an example — in which it could happen, and that he would not make a blanket promise that it never would.

Blanche also stressed the other side of the line. He said the department does not intend to improperly interfere with elections or with state certification, and that he is not planning his days around being somewhere to stop a certification. Under the Constitution and federal law, running elections and certifying results belong to the states and Congress; the federal government has no formal role in state certification itself.

The remarks did not land in isolation. They came the same week the department sued to hold up certification of Alaska's Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses, sued California over ballots it says may come from noncitizens, and, according to Blanche, is looking at similar voting lawsuits against a number of other states. A federal judge has separately barred Homeland Security voter-fraud field operations in nine states through Election Day.

With 11 days left in the campaign, the open door is itself the story: even a hypothetical federal move against certification would be unprecedented in modern elections. Watch for any new filings before November 3, and for how state election officials respond to the comments.

items.title: Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 in his $10 billion BBC lawsuit
items.summary:
A federal judge in Florida has ordered President Donald Trump to answer questions under oath by December 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC, according to Associated Press reporting cited by Reuters. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett issued the order from the bench at a hearing on Thursday, after the broadcaster accused Trump of stalling in a case he himself brought.

The lawsuit, filed in Florida federal court last December, claims a BBC documentary misleadingly spliced together separate parts of Trump's January 6, 2021 speech to make it look as if he directly urged supporters to storm the Capitol. The BBC has acknowledged the edit was misleading and apologized, while denying it amounts to defamation. Trump had been scheduled for a deposition in October but canceled, citing the demands of the presidency.

Discovery has become the battleground. The BBC is seeking financial records from Trump's Mar-a-Lago club and related business entities, arguing they are needed to test his damages claims; his lawyers call the requests overly broad and say they are not avoiding testimony, only managing a president's schedule and security needs. Reporting on the hearing said failure to comply could bring sanctions up to dismissal of the suit, unless the presiding judge extends discovery.

The case is one of several Trump has filed against news organizations whose coverage he disputes. Watch the December 11 deadline, the separate fight over whether former special counsel Jack Smith can testify, and the BBC's argument that the case does not belong in a U.S. court at all.

items.title: Virginia's Senate president pro tempore indicted in an alleged $4.5 million marijuana racketeering scheme
items.summary:
Federal prosecutors announced Thursday that Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, one of the most powerful Democrats in Richmond, has been indicted with six co-defendants in an alleged bribery and racketeering scheme built around a cannabis business she co-owns in Portsmouth. Lucas surrendered and was taken into federal custody with the others, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters in Norfolk.

The indictment, filed October 14 in the Eastern District of Virginia, charges conspiracy to distribute marijuana, conspiracy to launder money, money laundering, and bribery, alleging large quantities of illegal marijuana were sold under the cover of her legal medical cannabis business. FBI Director Kash Patel put the alleged scheme at about $4.5 million and said Lucas used her post chairing the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield it. The co-defendants include two of her daughters and a grandson, and the FBI had searched her office and the shop back in May.

Lucas, 82, has served in the Virginia Senate since 1991 and is its president pro tempore. She answered on social media that she would fight back, invoking her upbringing under Jim Crow and saying she would not be intimidated or bullied. As with any indictment, the charges are allegations and the defendants are presumed innocent.

The case lands in the middle of Virginia's redistricting and cannabis-policy fights, where Lucas has been a central figure and a vocal Trump critic — a context her defenders are already citing. Watch her first court appearances, whether she steps back from her committee role, and how state Democrats handle a leader under federal indictment.

items.title: Mississippi's attorney general orders a Senate candidate to pull an AI video of his opponent
items.summary:
Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch moved on Friday to force Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom to take down an artificial-intelligence-generated video of his opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Fitch said the posts appear to violate Mississippi's 2024 law against using deepfakes to influence an election, and warned her office could seek a court injunction if they stayed up.

The video shows a figure resembling Hyde-Smith fleeing reporters and dodging questions about health care and a much-discussed interview answer about protein. Neither the video nor its social media captions disclosed that it was made with AI; instead the captions called it based on a true story. State Republican chair Mike Hurst filed the complaint on Thursday, arguing that passing off a manufactured video as real in the final weeks of a campaign is deception, not satire or parody, which the law leaves room for.

Colom agreed to delete the posts on Friday, saying he would not spend taxpayer hard-earned dollars on costly litigation — while pushing back that the video was clearly parody and accusing Hyde-Smith's allies of weaponizing the justice system to change the subject. Mississippi's law covers realistic digital recreations released within 90 days of an election and carries criminal penalties for violations.

The episode is an early test of how far state deepfake laws reach when a campaign labels obvious parody as a true story instead of labeling it as AI. Watch whether Fitch's office pursues the matter further after the takedown, and whether other campaigns in the final stretch pull or relabel AI content pre-emptively.

items.title: Trump lifts some 50% tariffs on Canada, in a move aimed at helping Susan Collins in Maine
items.summary:
The United States moved on Friday to exempt some Canadian products from 50 percent tariffs, a step the Wall Street Journal reports is intended in part to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins and other Republicans in the closing days of the midterm campaign. The changes take effect October 30.

Relief covers certain products used in agriculture, including some machinery and refrigeration equipment, plus packaging and plywood sheets, according to documents posted on the White House website. The same action is not a one-way easing: a 50 percent tariff will be placed on other Canadian goods at the same time, including carpet, certain valves, and waste products.

Collins, who has broken with President Donald Trump over tariffs, praised the move and said she had pressed the administration for relief from costs hitting Maine businesses and families, while calling for a broader trade agreement with Canada. Her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, has made the trade war with Canada a centerpiece of his campaign, and polls show the two neck-and-neck in a state whose economy is deeply tied to Canadian trade.

The backdrop is a fight that escalated in late August, when Trump applied 50 percent tariffs to about $20 billion in Canadian goods — roughly 5 percent of Canada's exports to the U.S. — after last-minute talks broke down, and Canada retaliated. Watch whether more exemptions follow before Election Day, and whether tariff relief this targeted moves Maine voters or simply underlines how central trade has become in the race.

items.title: Wall Street ends the week lower as oil jumps and the Dow drops more than 600 points
items.summary:
Stocks closed lower on Friday, with the selling spreading beyond the technology names that led Thursday's slide. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 percent, to 52,215.16 — its worst day since August in some coverage — while the S&P 500 lost 0.52 percent to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.21 percent to 25,955.34 after briefly rebounding at midday. For the week the Dow still managed a small gain, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq finished lower.

Energy was the clear driver in the other direction. West Texas Intermediate crude settled about 3.8 percent higher near $103 a barrel and Brent rose about 3.1 percent to around $116.72, lifting energy shares about 2.5 percent while consumer staples, communication services and consumer discretionary lagged. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed back to 5.00 percent, and the VIX rose to 19.45, keeping pressure on rate-sensitive stocks.

The close matters because it changes the story from a narrow AI pullback to a broader risk-off week. Thursday was about Meta's spending and doubts over AI returns; Friday added oil, yields and Middle East supply fears on top, just ahead of the Federal Reserve meeting and a heavy week of Big Tech earnings.

Watch next week in order: the Fed decision on Wednesday, then Microsoft and Alphabet that same day and Amazon and others after. If oil stays above $100 and yields stay at 5 percent, even strong earnings may have to fight the macro backdrop.

items.title: Instacart explores a sale, with Uber and DoorDash named as early suitors
items.summary:
Instacart is exploring a possible sale and has held preliminary talks with Uber and DoorDash, The Information reported on Friday, in a story picked up by Reuters late in the session. Instacart shares closed about 9 percent higher on the news, while Uber fell nearly 3 percent and DoorDash dropped more than 4 percent. None of the three companies confirmed a deal — Instacart declined to comment and the other two did not immediately respond.

Instacart, legally Maplebear, carries a market value of roughly $12 billion. Using a typical takeover premium for public technology deals of 30 to 40 percent, the reporting put a possible price around $16 billion to $17 billion. That is well below the $40 billion to $50 billion range discussed when DoorDash last explored buying Instacart in 2021, when Instacart's private valuation was near $39 billion and those talks fell apart in part over antitrust concerns.

A combination would give either buyer a much stronger grocery business — Instacart's retailer relationships and marketplace paired with a larger delivery network — but it would also concentrate two of the biggest U.S. food-delivery platforms and is expected to draw close antitrust scrutiny. Uber has already been consolidating the sector, including a nearly $15 billion deal in July for Germany's Delivery Hero.

Watch for any company confirmation, a formal strategic-review statement, or a regulatory signal. For now this is preliminary discussions with no guarantee of a transaction.

items.title: Big banks move to block outside AI agents from customer accounts
items.summary:
Major U.S. banks are racing to limit third-party AI agents that can log into customer accounts, according to an Axios report described in Friday follow-on coverage. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking outside agents from its platforms, and JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo have also restricted access in varying ways, with many banks pushing agents toward read-only use so they cannot make changes.

The immediate issue, as described by people familiar with the matter, is less an agent breaking in on its own than customers handing their own usernames and passwords to AI tools. Once an agent acts with those credentials, a bank can struggle to tell whether a transaction, a settings change or even a call-center contact reflects the customer's instruction or the agent going beyond it. A Chase spokesperson warned customers not to share login credentials with anyone, including AI agents, and JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned on an earnings call that thousands of rogue agents could be operating across financial platforms.

Coverage also noted a consumer-protection consequence: customers who hand over credentials may have little claim to restitution under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act if something goes wrong. That turns a convenience choice — letting an agent check balances, move money or make purchases — into a liability question for the customer as well as the bank.

Watch how banks formalize the distinction between viewing information and taking action. Read-only access, per-action confirmation and a clear record of who authorized what are likely to become the baseline for any agent that touches money.

items.title: Cybersecurity stocks rally as a critical PHP flaw forces government sites offline
items.summary:
Cybersecurity shares extended their rally on Friday after a severe vulnerability in PHP, the language behind a large share of websites, disrupted government sites in Europe and elsewhere. CrowdStrike closed up 8.25 percent at $257.57 in market data for the session, while TradingKey's Friday tally showed Palo Alto Networks up about 6.6 percent, Okta about 6.3 percent, Cloudflare about 6.0 percent, Datadog about 5.0 percent and Zscaler about 4.9 percent during the move.

Reuters reporting cited in the coverage said some operators took sites offline after failing to patch before hackers could exploit the flaw. The PHP project disclosed two critical remote-code-execution flaws on October 21 and said upgrading is the only complete fix. Security professionals quoted in the coverage linked the episode to a broader shift: AI tools are finding vulnerabilities faster, with threat-intelligence firm VulnCheck research pointing to a year-over-year doubling in discoveries.

Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince warned that many other critical flaws in widely used software are still being patched and that turbulence could last for years. Deutsche Bank analysts added that rising AI use itself increases demand for the infrastructure and security firms that protect it, naming names such as CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks as potential beneficiaries, while noting some of that upside is already in valuations.

Watch patching progress on the PHP flaws and whether enterprises actually accelerate security budgets, rather than this remaining a one-week trade on a single vulnerability.

items.title: Business activity stays strong in October, but selling prices rise at the fastest pace since 2022
items.summary:
U.S. private-sector activity kept expanding in October, according to S&P Global's flash survey released Friday. The composite PMI eased to 57.6 from 58.4 in September — still the second-sharpest increase since March 2022 — with services at 57.9 and manufacturing rising to 56.0, a 53-month high. New orders rose at the fastest pace in more than four and a half years, export orders improved, and hiring was the second-fastest in over four years, with factory hiring the strongest since March 2012.

The inflation side of the survey was the headline for markets. Selling prices across goods and services rose at the sharpest rate since August 2022, with the prices-charged index at 59.8, while input costs rose at a pace second only to September since November 2022. Supplier delivery times deteriorated the most in more than four years, and backlogs grew, making it easier for firms to pass costs through.

S&P Global chief business economist Chris Williamson said the output readings are consistent with GDP growing at about a 5 percent annualized rate after a strong third quarter, but he flagged the renewed surge in oil prices as a key cost concern and said the price pace points to consumer inflation rising further above the Fed's target.

That combination — booming activity plus re-accelerating prices — is awkward for the Fed meeting next week. It supports holding rates steady to fight inflation rather than cutting, and it helps explain why yields rose back to 5 percent on Friday.

items.title: Procter & Gamble beats estimates, then falls as its cost burden jumps to $1.4 billion
items.summary:
Procter & Gamble shares fell about 2.6 percent on Friday to around $161.25, even though the consumer-products giant had beaten quarterly expectations the day before. The company reported net sales of $23.28 billion, up 4 percent from a year earlier and ahead of roughly $22.8 billion expected, with core earnings of $2.00 a share, up just 1 percent and above consensus around $1.89. Organic sales rose 4 percent, with volume contributing 2.4 points and all ten product categories growing.

The problem was converting those sales into profit. Core gross margin fell 150 basis points and operating margin fell 80 basis points despite large productivity savings, as inflation, freight, energy and raw-material costs weighed. Management raised its expected fiscal 2027 after-tax commodity-cost headwind to about $1.4 billion, up from $1 billion — a 40 percent increase — plus additional pressure from interest expense and foreign exchange.

P&G maintained its full-year organic sales guidance of 1 to 3 percent growth and core earnings guidance of $6.89 to $7.11 a share, and it raised all-in sales guidance to 2 to 4 percent to reflect its October 1 acquisition of wellness brand Thorne. Investors focused instead on the gap between 4 percent sales growth and 1 percent earnings growth.

For households, the story is a familiar one in corporate form: demand for everyday staples is holding up and shoppers are buying more volume, but the companies making those products are still passing through — or absorbing — higher input costs. Watch the November 19 investor day for whether P&G signals more pricing, more cost cuts, or both.

items.title: Justice Department sues to block Alaska from certifying its Senate race if the Republican loses
items.summary:
The Justice Department sued on Thursday to preemptively block Alaska from certifying its U.S. Senate result if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses by a narrow margin, arguing voters could be confused by another candidate with a nearly identical name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. President Trump told reporters on Friday that he directed the filing, saying he was the one who said to do it. The suit asks a federal judge in Anchorage to hold certification pending an investigation into whether votes for the second Sullivan were meant for the senator.

The race could decide control of the Senate. Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former U.S. representative, in a close contest where polling has shown her tied or slightly ahead in a state Trump carried by about 14 points in 2024. The department alleges the other Sullivan is running with the intention of misleading supporters; he has denied that aim, says he wants to unseat the senator and put Alaska first, and will appear on the ballot without a party designation after the Alaska Supreme Court allowed his candidacy in June.

Legal experts reacted sharply. David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research said the administration has no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify, and noted the ballot issue was already litigated in state courts. Notre Dame election-law professor Derek Muller called the legal argument one of the worst he has seen and said it appears designed to win a press release rather than the litigation.

No election has been held yet and no result is being overturned — this is a conditional request tied to a future loss. Watch for Alaska's response and whether a judge is willing to intervene before November 3 in how a state certifies a federal election.

items.title: Trump ally Corey Lewandowski faces a criminal investigation over his DHS work
items.summary:
Corey Lewandowski, a longtime Trump political adviser who served as a top aide at the Department of Homeland Security, is under criminal investigation over allegations he profited from his government role, Reuters reported, citing three U.S. officials and a fourth person familiar with the matter. The inquiry began with a criminal referral to the Justice Department from DHS's internal watchdog, whose office has been examining Lewandowski's involvement in certain government contracts.

Lewandowski's lawyer told the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the probe, that his client denies all allegations of wrongdoing, and told other outlets he has not been contacted by the Justice Department. Reuters reported the department has not yet issued subpoenas or other legal demands, and all of its sources spoke anonymously. The Justice Department and DHS did not provide substantive public comment in the coverage.

The case stands out because investigations of people close to Trump have been rare in this administration, which has more visibly pursued prominent critics of the president and moved to dismiss several cases involving allies. Asked about the reports, Trump said he did not know the specifics but wanted his people to be honest and would have the Justice Department act if they were not.

This is an early-stage investigation, not a charge. Watch for whether prosecutors issue subpoenas, which U.S. attorney's office takes the lead, and what the inspector general's contracting review ultimately documents.

items.title: Justice Department asks an appeals court to block California from counting 20,000 ballots
items.summary:
The Justice Department asked a federal appeals court on Thursday to intervene in its lawsuit seeking to temporarily block California from counting more than 20,000 mail-in ballots. The ballots come from voters the Trump administration alleges are likely not U.S. citizens.

The appeal escalates a fight that began when the department sent California officials a list of about 20,000 voters it says should have their ballots set aside, and sued after the state and Los Angeles County refused. California officials have defended their voter rolls and their handling of the list.

The case is one of several election lawsuits the administration is pursuing in the final stretch before the November 3 midterms, alongside a suit over Alaska's Senate certification and court limits on Homeland Security voter-fraud field operations in nine states. Each tests how far the federal government can go in second-guessing state-run elections.

Watch for the appeals court's timeline: any order would have to land quickly to affect counting, and California is expected to argue that blocking ballots this close to an election would disenfranchise eligible voters caught up in list errors.

items.title: Top RFK Jr. adviser Calley Means quits, and the MAHA alliance with Trump frays
items.summary:
Calley Means, a senior adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and one of the best-known figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from the Trump administration on October 22. In his statement he praised President Trump and Kennedy and said the movement is in the first inning and just getting started.

Behind the courteous exit, reporting describes mounting frustration that MAHA's core food and health priorities have stalled. A breaking point, according to officials cited in coverage, was the postponement of a meeting on defining ultraprocessed foods — the groundwork for possible regulation of sweeteners and additives — along with repeated delays to a school lunch rule, which officials attributed to industry concerns. Means had worked on revamped dietary guidelines, voluntary artificial-dye removal by major food companies, and restrictions on sugary drinks under SNAP in 17 states.

The resignation lands on a coalition already grading the administration harshly. Earlier this month a group of MAHA activists released a scorecard rating 42 administration promises and found none fully kept, five partially kept and 37 broken, and prominent MAHA voices say supporters feel their priorities were rented for the 2024 campaign rather than adopted.

Why it matters: MAHA voters helped power Trump's return to the White House, and their disillusionment is surfacing 11 days before midterms that will decide how much of the health agenda can move at all. Watch whether Kennedy publicly fills Means's role, and whether the ultraprocessed-food definition and school lunch rule move or stall further.

items.title: New York City votes to end horse-drawn carriages in Central Park by 2028
items.summary:
The New York City Council voted 40 to 7 on October 22 to ban horse-drawn carriages, phasing out a tradition that has run in and around Central Park since the 1800s. The ban takes full effect in June 2028, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani supports the bill and is expected to sign it.

Council Speaker Julie Menin said the vote reflects a commitment to animal welfare, public safety and protecting workers. The push intensified this summer after 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan was killed in June when he was thrown from a carriage, and after a carriage horse collapsed in Central Park. The city has long limited carriage licenses to 68, and the rides became a tourism staple featured in films from Sex and the City to Elf and Home Alone 2.

Animal-rights groups have argued for years that the horses endure harsh, unnatural conditions and physical exhaustion in city traffic. Carriage drivers counter that the animals are cared for and warn about their own livelihoods, which is why the legislation pairs the phase-out with attention to workers as well as horses.

President Trump, a New Yorker, criticized the decision and called the carriages a great tradition that will be missed. Watch for the mayor's signature, the city's transition plan for drivers, and where the horses go once the last licenses wind down in 2028.

items.title: PG&E warns of possible weekend power shutoffs across seven Northern California counties
items.summary:
Pacific Gas & Electric warned Friday that it may cut power to parts of seven Northern California counties beginning Friday night to reduce wildfire risk as strong offshore winds move in. The utility estimated about 644 customers could be affected across Butte, Lake, Napa, Shasta, Solano, Sonoma and Yolo counties, with shutoffs possibly starting as early as 7 p.m. Friday and some outages lasting until Saturday night.

Forecast gusts of 40 to 60 miles per hour, combined with low humidity, are the concern, especially in the North Bay hills and northern Sierra foothills late Friday into Saturday morning. PG&E meteorologists said recent rain helped in some places but was limited in exactly those drier areas, leaving brush highly flammable despite the wet weather elsewhere in the region.

These public-safety shutoffs are a preventive tool California utilities have used since the state's catastrophic wildfire seasons: de-energizing lines in high-risk weather so damaged or wind-blown equipment is less likely to spark a fire. The tradeoff is immediate disruption for the households and businesses that lose power, including medical-device users and people without backup supply.

Watch PG&E's final shutoff map and restoration timeline through Saturday, and National Weather Service wind and humidity updates for the North Bay and Sierra foothills, which will decide whether the warning becomes a wider outage.

items.title: Election forecasters now favor Amy Acton for governor after the attack-ad backlash
items.summary:
Two major nonpartisan election forecasters moved Ohio's governor's race in Democrat Amy Acton's direction on Friday. Both the Cook Political Report and Sabato's Crystal Ball changed their rating from a toss-up to leaning Democratic, a shift that followed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's decision to put serious money behind a deeply personal attack ad.

The ad features Acton's birth mother accusing her daughter of dishonesty about her childhood and urging voters to reject her. Acton has had no contact with her mother since she was 12, after her stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her and her mother lost custody. Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed it produced the spot and plans to spend about $4 million airing it, and on Friday he defended it at campaign stops, saying it was not about abuse and accusing the media of protecting Acton.

The reaction has split Ohio Republicans in public. Governor Mike DeWine, who has endorsed Ramaswamy, called the ad wrong and urged that it be taken down, while other senior Republicans said they would not have run it. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, and the campaign has refused to pull it.

Analysts say the episode confirmed a broader problem for Ramaswamy: a candidate who entered with Trump's backing and cleared the field has proved divisive, and recent polling already showed Acton gaining as cost-of-living concerns weighed on Republicans. Watch whether the new rating holds once the first polls taken entirely after the ad aired are released.

items.title: Early voting is surging in Ohio, with more than 920,000 ballots already cast
items.summary:
Ohio voters are turning out early at a pace well above recent midterms. More than 920,000 ballots had been cast statewide as of Friday, and in Franklin County alone the total passed 88,000, split almost evenly between in-person voting and returned mail ballots.

Franklin County's elections director said in-person early voting is running at more than twice the 2022 rate and is on track to pass the county's entire 2018 in-person total before the weekend is over. The shift reflects a broader pattern: mail voting has faded since its pandemic peak, while voters increasingly prefer to show up in person. Lines at the Franklin County board office reached about 45 minutes on Friday, though officials said they keep moving.

Election officials credit the close statewide races — Acton against Ramaswamy for governor and a heated U.S. Senate contest — for pulling voters in early rather than waiting for November 3.

For anyone planning to vote early, Saturday voting begins October 24, hours expand during the final week, and early in-person voting runs through November 1. Watch whether the early pace holds in Cuyahoga County and the suburbs, which will be a useful signal for overall turnout on Election Day.

items.title: U.S. Marshals arrest two wanted men in Northern Ohio, including a Cleveland murder suspect
items.summary:
A federal fugitive task force arrested two men in Northern Ohio on Friday. Jayden Lockett, 19, was taken into custody at an address on Hege Avenue in Cleveland, where officers also seized a firearm, and Stephen Imler, 29, was arrested at an address on Hametown Road in Norton.

Lockett was wanted by Cleveland police for aggravated murder in connection with a late-September shooting. Police responding to a shots-fired call near East 68th Street found two young men shot inside a vehicle on East 55th Street; the 22-year-old driver was shot twice in the head and later died, while a 21-year-old passenger was wounded in the leg and survived.

Imler, a former high school band director and music teacher in Stark County, was wanted on three counts of sexual battery and two counts of grooming. He was placed on leave in August after allegations surfaced, resigned in early September, and was charged afterward.

The arrests matter locally because both cases had been open for weeks with suspects at large. Both men now face court proceedings on the underlying charges, and the Marshals are continuing to solicit tips on other wanted fugitives through their Northern Ohio task force line.

items.title: Senator Husted brings NASA's administrator to Cleveland to showcase Ohio's space work
items.summary:
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman spent Friday in Cleveland at the invitation of U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, joining a roundtable with Ohio aerospace companies, universities and economic-development leaders before touring NASA Glenn Research Center.

The visit was built around Ohio's role in the Artemis Moon program. Glenn leads work on spacecraft mechanisms, structures and pyrotechnics for Artemis, and the agency's test facility in Sandusky — which can reproduce the vacuum and temperature extremes of space — was used to test the Orion capsule ahead of the Artemis II launch. The tour also covered Glenn's nuclear research programs.

Husted used the visit to point to funding and policy wins he has backed for the center, including full NASA funding in the current appropriations bill, support for Glenn's Fission Surface Power work on a lunar nuclear reactor, and $110 million directed toward nuclear propulsion systems that Glenn will lead. Defense legislation he supported also encourages the Pentagon to use existing hypersonic test facilities in Sandusky rather than building duplicates.

For Northeast Ohio, the stakes are jobs and long-term federal investment: Glenn is one of the region's anchor research employers, and programs assigned there tend to support local suppliers and university research for years. Watch for any follow-on commitments from NASA about workload or staffing at Glenn after the visit.

items.title: Ohio measles cases reach 260 across 24 counties, though the weekly pace is slowing
items.summary:
Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 is still growing, but more slowly. The state health department's latest dashboard, updated October 22, reports 260 cases across 24 counties so far this year, with eight new cases in the past week — down sharply from 24 new cases the week before. Van Wert County, in western Ohio, reported its first case.

The geographic pattern remains concentrated in northeast and north-central Ohio. Geauga County has the most cases at 54, followed by Wayne at 45 and Ashtabula at 44, with smaller clusters in Harrison, Medina and Tuscarawas counties. Cuyahoga County has recorded three cases this year. Health officials say the overwhelming majority of people infected have been unvaccinated, and confirmed ages have ranged from toddlers to young adults.

The state total is now nearly five times the 45 cases Ohio recorded in all of 2025, part of a national resurgence that has pushed U.S. cases to their highest level in 35 years. Ohio's childhood MMR vaccination coverage has slipped below the level health officials consider necessary to stop spread in a community.

For families, the practical guidance from the state is unchanged: two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective, and anyone with fever and rash who may have been exposed should call a provider before arriving in person. Watch the next weekly dashboard update for whether the slower pace holds or the new Van Wert case signals spread into a new region.

items.title: Browns get Mason Graham and Quinshon Judkins back for Sunday's game at Tennessee
items.summary:
Cleveland's final injury report before Sunday's trip to Tennessee brought mostly good news. Defensive tackle Mason Graham, who missed the last couple of games with a knee injury, carries no injury designation and will play, and running back Quinshon Judkins is also back after missing the last game.

Graham's return is the headline. He has already recorded four sacks this season as a disruptive interior presence, and Cleveland's defense managed to keep pressuring quarterbacks without him — adding him back strengthens the unit's strongest area. Judkins' return restores the Browns' lead rushing option for a road game they are favored to win.

Four Browns remain questionable: safety Grant Delpit, working through concussion protocol; cornerback Denzel Ward, limited Friday by a hand injury; linebacker Quincy Williams; and running back Dylan Sampson, who has not played since a Week 1 injury put him on injured reserve. Ward and Williams are both expected to be available. Four players were ruled out, including defensive tackle Mike Hall Jr. and quarterback Dillon Gabriel, neither a current starter.

At 4-2 and alone in first place in the AFC North, Cleveland has a chance to reach 5-2 against a 1-5 Titans team before a harder stretch of road games. Watch the final inactive list Sunday morning, particularly for Delpit and Ward in the secondary.

baby.tip: Paperwork and go-bag week: do one final hospital-bag check together — IDs and insurance cards, phone chargers, snacks and a change of clothes for Mike, and a going-home outfit for the baby in two sizes, since newborn and 0-3 month fits vary a lot. Put the bag by the door and the car seat base check on the same list, and if anything about pre-registration or where to check in is unclear, ask your OB's office this week while it's still a calm question.
baby.fact: Newborns arrive already knowing the sounds of home. Babies can recognize their mother's voice at birth from hearing it in the womb, and they are calmed by familiar voices and rhythms — which is why talking, humming, and reading to the baby now, and in those first days, genuinely registers.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for today: start the family birth pool, just for fun. Mike, Kelly, and the grandparents each write down a predicted date, time, and weight, seal them in an envelope, and open it together after the baby arrives. Closest guess picks the first celebratory takeout order.
